use(store) and Context

At the same compiler setting, use(store) matches or beats a context per slice in every configuration, with the compiler and without it. It matches or beats one context in 35 of 42 configurations with the compiler, and loses by at most 11% in the rest. Where every row reads the value that changed, use(store) and one context re-render the same rows.

use(store) vs Context at the same compiler setting. Bold: matched or beaten.

Against one context, the big wins are where few components read the change: editing one entity, and the conditional reads.

These are synthetic benchmarks with no data from a real app yet, and use(store) is an experiment that hasn't shipped (see method and caveats).

What the three approaches are, and the ranges

The three approaches put the same state in different places:

  • One context (context) holds all the state in a useReducer at the root and passes it down through one Provider.
  • A context per slice (context-split) gives each slice of state its own Provider, and wraps rows in memo, the way people usually do.
  • use(store) (store) puts each entity in its own store, with small stores for the selection, the filter, the expanded rows, and the details.

Each comparison below pits use(store) against one Context approach at the same compiler setting: both without the compiler, or both with it.

  • Without the compiler, use(store) against one context is 1.05× slower to 57× faster (24 faster, 15 tie, 3 slower), and against a context per slice it's up to 62× faster (40 faster, 2 tie).
  • With the compiler, against one context it's 1.1× slower to 9.3× faster (30 faster, 5 tie, 7 slower), and against a context per slice it's 1.1–11× faster.
  • Where every row reads the change, they're close without the compiler. With it, use(store) pulls ahead on add / remove (1.3–2.2× faster), and one context wins some filter and subscribe churn configurations.

This page compares use(store) with Context, with and without the React Compiler for each. It uses the same results as the benchmark report, which compares use(store) with Redux and Zustand, and has the full method. For how a store differs from Context, read differences from useState and Context in the explainer.

Why the approaches differ

The timing mostly follows the renders. Where use(store) renders fewer rows and views, it wins by a lot.

The counting build shows the difference at 1,000 rows. It counts renders of Row, RowView, DetailsView, and CountView, not every component. Editing one entity re-renders 1 row with use(store), and 1,000 with one context or with a context per slice, because every row reads the entities. Changing the selection re-renders every row in all three (1,000), because every row reads the selection.

Work for one update in the counting build (1,000 rows). Counted renders are the renders of Row, RowView, DetailsView, and CountView, not every component (App and the list aren't counted). Row renders are among them. Context re-renders every consumer of a changed value. With the compiler, unchanged output is skipped.

Why

Context re-renders every component that reads a context when the context's value changes. A context per slice narrows that to the consumers of the slice that changed. use(store) re-renders only the components that read the store that changed. The explainer covers the problem with Context and what re-renders.

Where all three render every row, the gaps are smaller, but they don't follow the render counts. With the compiler, use(store) is 1.3–2.2× faster on add / remove against one context, with the same rows rendered.

The conditional reads are the exception. A context per slice re-renders as few rows and views as use(store) there, and use(store) is still faster: 1.9–2.5× faster on the inline read with the compiler. When a context's value changes, React searches the tree below the Provider for its consumers. A store update goes straight to its readers (see what re-renders). I think that search is most of the difference, along with the root re-rendering to update its Providers on every change, but neither is profiled.

All the data →

Without the compiler, one context wins only in subscribe churn, by at most 5%.

  • Editing an entity: use(store) against one context is 20–57× faster.
  • The inline conditional read: 23–34× faster against one context, and 2.5–3.2× faster against a context per slice, whose rows are wrapped in memo.
  • Selection and filter tie one context in every configuration (6 of 6 and 6 of 6). In both scenarios every row reads the changed value, so both apps re-render every row and its children.
Why

Without the compiler, every component that re-renders also re-renders its children, unless they're wrapped in memo. That's where the difference in renders shows most.

All the data →

With the compiler, one context wins 7 configurations, in filter and subscribe churn, by at most 11%. A context per slice never wins.

  • Editing an entity: 3.1–9.3× faster against one context, and 3.7–11× faster against a context per slice.
  • Selection: up to 1.4× faster (2 faster, 4 tie) against one context.
  • Add / remove: 1.3–2.2× faster against one context. Every variant re-renders every row here, so it mostly measures list reconciliation.
Why

With the compiler, a component that re-renders returns its cached elements when their inputs didn't change, so its children don't re-render. That helps all three. It shrinks the big gaps (entity edits and the conditional reads) and widens some small ones, like add / remove.

What the compiler buys each approach. Bold: faster or tied with it.

The compiler helps one context far more than use(store) on entity edits and the conditional reads, where one context re-renders many more components. It helps a context per slice far more only on entity edits.

  • One context: 3.1–12× faster.
  • A context per slice: 1.3–8.7× faster.
  • use(store): 1.1× slower to 13× faster (34 faster, 7 tie, 1 slower). It doesn't help on entity edits (6 tie), because only one row re-renders anyway. It's slower in the conditional read in a child component, by at most 9%.
Why, and how often it helps use(store) more

Where every row re-renders, it often speeds use(store) up more. Overall, it speeds use(store) up more than one context in 16 of 42 configurations, including every add / remove configuration (6.0–12× faster, against 4.9–6.0× faster for one context). Against a context per slice it's 22 of 42, including every configuration of selection, filter, and add / remove. These compare two speedups without a noise test, so read them as a direction. It never makes either Context approach slower.

On entity edits and the conditional reads, I think Context gains more because it re-renders more. Every component the compiler lets React skip is one that Context re-rendered, and that use(store) often didn't render at all.

Typing and memory

Without the compiler and with no CPU slowdown, one context's slowest one in twenty keys (p95) took 159.8 ms. use(store) took 12.6 ms, and a context per slice 15.7 ms.

All the data →

The compiler brought one context down to 20.5 ms. For use(store), the compiler made typing slower with no CPU slowdown (17.0 ms) and faster with a four times CPU slowdown (42.3 ms without it, 39.9 ms with it). I don't know why yet. The typing benchmark has far fewer samples than the main suite, so treat differences this small with care.

How typing was measured

The typing benchmark types into the filter while 10,000 expensive rows re-filter in a transition. All three update the list in a transition, so React can interrupt the list render to handle the next key. One context also holds the input's value, so the urgent update for each key re-renders every row that reads the context.

For memory, use(store) uses more per row than either Context approach. At the largest size with the compiler, it uses 1.34× the bytes per row of one context, and 1.29× those of a context per slice. The compiler adds bytes per row for all three. The benchmark report has the full tables.

All the data →

Where Context ties or wins

  • One context ties use(store) on selection and filter without the compiler, because both re-render every row and its children (2,000 counted renders with use(store) on a selection change, and 2,001 with one context).
  • One context wins 7 configurations with the compiler, in filter and subscribe churn, by at most 11%. In those scenarios every row reads the changed value with both, so they render the same components (1,502 against 1,502 on a filter change). The difference is in work the render counts don't show. In subscribe churn, that includes use(store) subscribing and unsubscribing the details readers.
  • Both Context approaches use less memory per row.
  • A context per slice never beats use(store) at the same compiler setting.

Method and caveats

The method is the same as the benchmark report's. It uses one frozen React build and times behind a gate on ambient CPU, except for the main suite's first restart, which ran under the load-average gate it replaced. Verdicts compare means and need every browser restart to agree. The counting build counts renders of the rows and the shared views. The benchmark report's method section has the details.

  • These are synthetic benchmarks, with no data from a real app.
  • Timing uses the production build, and each update runs inside flushSync. Only the typing benchmark measures what transitions do for responsiveness.
  • Add / remove is low-signal, because it mostly measures list reconciliation.
  • The Context apps are written the usual way: one useReducer and Provider, or a Provider per slice with memo rows. A Context app tuned with more splitting or more memo could do better.

How to reproduce

These results come from the same runs as the benchmark report, and its How to reproduce section has the commands.

Benchmarks: fixtures/store-bench. Context apps: fixtures/store-bench/src/apps/context.jsx and context-split.jsx. How it works: the explainer. Performance against Redux and Zustand: the benchmark report.
